stories.title: AI makes pull requests less central in open-source contribution
stories.summary: AI is shifting open-source contribution away from pull requests as the primary unit of value, particularly for utility software rather than mission-critical projects. While AI can generate most of the code a maintainer needs, it cannot determine what a project should become or evaluate UX trade-offs. As a result, the community's role is evolving from writing code to shaping project direction through precise, well-reproduced bug reports and thoughtful issue raising, which the author considers more valuable than unsolicited AI-generated pull requests. Looking ahead, the author predicts that every repository will eventually operate with a software factory running behind it, where execution begins automatically once a human approves a ready issue or pull request. Repositories will also need strong guidelines for feature requests and bug reports to streamline initial agentic assessment.
stories.snippet: Artificial intelligence is causing a shift in how contributions are made to open-source projects. The community's primary role will evolve from submitting code to defining project direction and providing valuable bug reports.

stories.title: Demystifying Kafka's Exactly-Once Semantics: Idempotence, Transactions, and Fencing
stories.summary: Kafka provides at-least-once delivery by default and achieves exactly-once delivery through three distinct layers. The first layer, producer idempotence, assigns each producer a unique Producer ID (PID) and attaches incrementing per-partition sequence numbers to message batches, allowing brokers to deduplicate retries from a single producer instance. The second layer addresses the "zombie instance" problem through user-defined transactional.id values paired with epochs, ensuring only the producer with the highest epoch can write and effectively fencing out stale instances. The third layer uses a Two-Phase Commit protocol managed by a Transaction Coordinator, with state stored in the internal __transaction_state topic, to enable atomic writes across multiple partitions. Importantly, Kafka guarantees exactly-once delivery and storage, not processing, so consumers must implement their own idempotency logic when exactly-once processing is required.
stories.snippet: Kafka's exactly-once semantics ensures messages are delivered and persisted exactly once, even in the face of retries and failures. This deep dive explores the three layers of its implementation: producer idempotence for single-producer retries, transactional IDs and epochs to handle zombie producers, and a distributed two-phase commit protocol for atomic writes across multiple partitions. It clarifies that this guarantee applies to delivery, not processing.

stories.title: Cloudflare Implements Cache Transcoding to Optimize Cache Storage with Zstandard
stories.summary: Cloudflare has implemented a technique called Cache Transcoding to optimize cache storage and reduce costs. When a response enters the cache, their proxy encodes the body using Zstandard compression before writing it to disk, keeping the data compressed while it remains cached and travels between data centers. The content is only decoded right before being delivered to the client. Cloudflare selectively applies this compression to text-based files such as HTML, CSS, JSON, and JavaScript, while skipping images and videos since these formats are already compressed and recompressing them would waste CPU resources. Using zstd level 3, they achieved a 2.8x reduction in size. The tradeoff favors this approach because cached assets are read far more often than they are written, making the small repeated decode cost worthwhile compared to the storage savings.
stories.snippet: Cloudflare employs Cache Transcoding, compressing text assets like HTML and CSS with Zstandard before caching them. This method significantly reduces storage and costs by accepting a small, repeated decode cost for frequently read cached data.

stories.title: Some more things about Django I've been enjoying
stories.summary: The author is learning Django to build traditional backend-rendered websites and appreciates several features. They enjoy Django's QuerySet pattern, defining custom methods like `approved()` or `future()` that chain together to create readable queries like `Events.objects.approved().for_tab(tab)`. They also find template filters such as `querystring` useful for generating links that modify URL parameters, and they praise Django's automatic database migrations, having completed 19 so far. While they find class-based view inheritance confusing and prefer function-based views, they don't mind using inheritance to interface with Django's own classes. Performance tuning revealed that an accidentally disabled cached template loader was a major bottleneck: enabling it improved throughput from roughly 2-3 to about 12 requests per second on a small VM. The author notes that starting with CPU profiling has been more helpful than chasing slow database queries, particularly because they use SQLite.

stories.title: Learning a few things about running SQLite
stories.summary: The author has been learning practical lessons about running SQLite as the database for a Django site, where the database is small (around 10,000 rows). After enabling WAL mode, a query using FTS5 full-text search on 4,000 rows took 5 seconds; running ANALYZE to generate statistics for the query planner reduced the time to about 0.05 seconds. Cleanup operations on unwanted rows have sometimes resulted in queries exceeding 5 seconds, which the author has handled by working in small batches. For backups, the author uses two methods: restic combined with sqlite3's "VACUUM INTO" command (though these have occasionally been killed and required unlocking), and more recently Litestream for incremental backups to AWS with a 400-hour retention setting. On a previous project, Mess with DNS, splitting tables into three separate database files proved helpful, and that site has run on SQLite successfully for four years since 2022.

stories.title: Show HN: TERMy – A fast terminal assistant that does not use LLMs
stories.summary: A developer frustrated with AI subscription costs for trivial terminal commands created TERMy, a fast terminal assistant that operates without large language models. After experiments with training transformers and Mamba architectures from scratch produced unsatisfactory results, the developer pivoted to a deterministic approach using NPC-Forge, a framework built around the NDF 0.0 dataset format. This format defines intents with vocabulary tags, named-entity regex patterns, and tool calls, allowing the system to match user input to predefined commands without any training. The core parser and runtime, FlintParser and FlintNPC, were implemented in roughly 1000 lines of code in both Python and JavaScript, running on CPU and responding in milliseconds. The developer argues that harnesses like Copilot should route trivial requests to deterministic NPCs like TERMy first, reserving heavy LLMs as a last resort to reduce compute waste.
stories.snippet: I love research and development, you may have heard of me because of PJON (Padded Jittering Operative Network). It is a network protocol I started developing in 2010, which was recently implemented in silicon by the ETH Zurich university thanks to the research of Pius Sieber. I am excited to share with you TERMy, a terminal assistant built on top of the NPC-Forge framework. Unlike everything else being built today, TERMy does not use embeddings, machine-learning or LLMs. It runs on the CPU (even on a Raspberry Pi Zero) both in the terminal or client-side in a browser tab and responds in milliseconds. It is a cynical but very knowledgeable Linux terminal assistant that translates your natural language into shell commands without relying on a single artificial neuron. I had a chance to focus for 2 months on my personal projects since early July, during the strange times of AI price hikes and the end of subsidized tokenmaxing. I was curious to see if I could develop from scratch a terminal assistant capable of handling simple natural language requests. I have a bad memory and got used to ask to copilot "activate the virtual environment" or similar trivial operations spending a non negligible sum every month. I started thinking, maybe I can do something to make my workflow more efficient? Do I really need trillions of parameters to accomplish those tasks? How it Works When you type a prompt, it goes through a lightweight NLU pipeline written in ~1000 lines of Python that implement the following steps: 1. Strip expletives, interjections, encouraging, discouraging and thanking words (remove noise) 2. Sentiment analysis 3. Exact Match (very fast) 4. Template Match (slower) 5. Probabilistic Match (even slower) Step 5 relies on: 1. IDF (Inverse Document Frequency) to identify rare words. 2. BOW (Bag Of Words) to accommodate word inversions. 3. IDF weighted Levenshtein to safely handle typos. Permission gating is hardcoded into the dataset and enforced for all potentially destructive commands, so it's inherently safer than letting an unpredictable LLM run wild on your machine. - TERMy in operation: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qeIp0xePLBg - Variance and typo tolerance: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tQvGDk6fkk0 - Copilot integration: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wzzouhq2a8A - Advanced features: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qeIp0xePLBg - Source Code: https://github.com/gioblu/NPC-Forge

stories.title: Trusting-Trust Attack against an Entire Linux Distribution (via the strip utility)
stories.summary: This paper demonstrates a "Trusting-Trust" style supply chain attack that compromises an entire Linux distribution by injecting malicious code into the `strip` utility from GNU binutils. Because `strip` processes nearly every compiled binary during package builds, a tampered version silently implants backdoors into the distribution's packages while leaving source code untouched and reproducible. Engineers and security teams should care because this attack bypasses source code audits and reproducible build defenses, proving that even carefully reviewed supply chains remain vulnerable to compromised toolchain binaries.
stories.snippet: "Ken Thompson's trusting-trust attack, in which a compromised compiler backdoors the programs it builds and reproduces the backdoor in subsequent rebuilds of itself, is widely regarded as a threat specific to compilers. We show that it is not." A few weeks ago I came across this https://www.teamten.com/lawrence/writings/coding-machines/ : it's clearly fictional (and furthermore is "pre-AI" in that it was written in 2009) but is interesting in that it raises the question of whether one or more computers could- without "intention" embed code meeting the "trusting trust" criteria in GCC.

stories.title: Surviving Code Reviews in the era of AI
stories.summary: The article addresses how to cope with code reviews when coworkers use AI to produce pull requests averaging 6,000 lines of diff, far too large to review effectively. Commenters recommend enforcing firm size limits (around 400 lines), rejecting oversized PRs, and breaking large changes into stacked PRs, where LLMs can help split work despite being mediocre at choosing good splits. AI review tools should be used only as a first pass, since LLM-generated explanations tend to be verbose, jargon-packed, and inconsistent. Effective personal strategies include teaching coworkers review standards directly, requiring plain-language PR descriptions explaining purpose and reasoning, and asking management to clarify review expectations. If the workplace culture won't accommodate these changes, the article warns you may be at a "slop company" and suggests considering whether to stay or leave.
stories.snippet: My coworkers are all fully AI pilled. As a consequence, every PR that comes my way for review is on average ~6k lines of diff. It's well established that even PRs an order of magnitude smaller than this are too big to be effectively reviewed. I'm still clinging to the idea that us humans should understand how the systems we are building work, so I'm hesitant to use AI for reviews aside from more general question answering. Much of what it produces in the way of explanations are difficult to follow and overly verbose anyway. I'm sure I'm not the only person here who has been dealing with this problem, so I'm curious if anyone here has found any strategies (organizational or personal) which have helped weather this maelstrom.

stories.title: Bespoke: A Programming Language for People Who Say Please
stories.summary: Bespoke is a proposed statically and nominally typed programming language in which all interactions with the compiler, output console, and host environment must use formal, courteous phrasing. Source files use the .charming extension, British spelling is enforced, and types must be written in full. Boolean literals are limited to Quite True and Patently False, while direct mutation like carriageCount = 42 produces diagnostic B-101 ("Blunt Imperative") and halts compilation. Control flow is ceremonial: if-statements pose hypothetical questions before the court, functions are introduced as diplomatic proposals, and exceptions are raised as awkward predicaments or regrettable circumstances. Memory management requires a formal request to the "groundskeeper," and mutexes are framed as requests for exclusive audience; deadlocks are recorded as "Exemplary Stalements of Mutual Deference." The author presents Bespoke as a satirical proposal, unrelated to Josiah Winslow's 2025 esolang of the same name.
